speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Pardon me?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Bunney.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Did you have any nicknames that you'd care to tell us?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: I used to. They used to call me "Tiny," but I sure ain't tiny anymore!

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Your date of birth?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: December 25, 1896.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: And the place of birth?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: You mean the town or state?

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Town or state, either one, both I guess.

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Well, I was born near a country store, the name of Mascot, Nebraska; but the post office was Oxford.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: That's fine. And where was the first place you lived in Idaho?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: In Princeton. I moved from Nebraska to Kansas.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: And did you move from Kansas out to Idaho?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: I was only in Nebraska three years.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Oh, you just came out really young then?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Yes . When I was 15, I came out from Kansas to Idaho.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: And do you know the approximate year that you came out to Idaho?

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: 1912, okay. How did you come out? EC : By train. My father bought a coach or a boxcar with the household goods and things in it.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: And any companions on this trip?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: My mother and father , sister and one brother , grandmother and grandfather .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Okay. What was your mother's maiden name?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Zeiger.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Do you know her date of birth?

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Do you know where she was born?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Missouri.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: And the date of her death?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: 1963, I don't know just the date .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Oh, that's okay, the year is fine. Do you know her occupation or jobs that she had?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Just a housewife .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: That's fine . Any chance, the year that she married?

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Your father's name?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Charles Elmer Bunney; we call him both names .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: And the date of his birth?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: October 20, 1866.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: The place of his birth?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Missouri.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: When did he die?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: I can't remember.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: That's all right, it's not necessary that you give us his death. His occupation or jobs?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Farmer.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Any brothers or sisters?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: I had one sister and two brothers .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: What were their names?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Mary was my sister, and Glen and Preston.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: I think I've got another page of stuff here. Your husband's name?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Eugene.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Occupation or jobs he had?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Farmer.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Date of his birth?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: February 3, 1896.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Place of his birth?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Princeton.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: What year did he die?

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Do you have the date and the place you were married?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Moscow.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Moscow? What was the date? EC : May 14, 1919. Were were married in the parsonage over there and it still stands .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Oh really, that's nice. And children's names?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Foy, Marlin, Charles, and Duane.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Their occupations?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Foy is now working on construction work; Marlin is a logger; Charles is down at the mill; and Duane is at Potlatch.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Date or place of birth?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Well, Duane was born in Moscow at the hospital .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: And the rest were born at home?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Charles was born in the Potlatch hospital . They were born 1920, 1925, 1930, and 1935.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: That's easy to remember. Could you tell me your education?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Eighth grade.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Eighth grade? A little personal information about you or any certain kinds of skills that you have? Well, I see that quilting is an important skill. I'll write that down.

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Quilting and crocheting.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Oh, wow!

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: And collecting.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: What do you like to collect?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: I just started teaching . This gentleman made my board up there the other day .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Oh!

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Water glasses, 50 vases in there.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Clubs, groups or societies that you belong to, church organizations?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: I belonged to a quilting club, Princeton Community Club, the Rebekah Lodge, Royal Neighbor, VFW, and the Grange .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: My goodness . EC : Belonged to the Butte over in Moscow. That's all , I guess .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: That's a lot. Occupations or jobs that you've held in your life?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Housewife. I filled in for the depot agent in Princeton once.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Any awards , honors or ribbons that you've won? Entered anything?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: There's my ribbons on the curtain in there.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Oh my goodness .

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Crocheting and some quilts . It won a few state ribbons and it went national, once.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Do you remember your childhood? Do you feel like you were treated differently than your brothers, that they had different chores than you did as a child, that you had to do?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: It's my brother, my older brother. He was older than I was , two years and he was sickly lots of times . I was an outdoor girl, my sister was an indoor girl . She done the inside work, I took care of chickens and milked cows .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: That was what you preferred?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Yes .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Rather than being indoors? Do you see families nowadays as different or similar to families when you were a girl?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Not particularly, it's all about the same. They have lots more going on and things . More was done in going to school and lots more than I used to do . But, my first day of school was a sod schoolhouse.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Did you dance?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: We danced.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: That's interesting.

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: We went to school three months in one district and three months in another because we couldn't afford a teacher in both of them, so we went in fall in one and in spring in another .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: What sort of social class did you see yourself in? Was there about the same as all your neighbors around you or in a different class?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: It was about the same, just about the same. I don't know, we just went to parties and danced at basket suppers and things like that .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: How long did you know the man that you married before you married him?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: We came in 1912 and I met him in 1919. He was in the service, that ' s the only time he left the place was while he was in the service.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: What basis did you decide to get married? Why did you decide to get married?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Well, we just went together four years and all of a sudden it got to be a habit. He had to go in the service, you know, and he got that discharge in March and we were married in May.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: How did your parents feel about the man you wanted to marry? Did they like him?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Yes .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Did you do anything unusual or anything that you'd like to tell about that we might be interested in when you were courting, different than what we might do nowadays?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Well, we always went for buggy rides, sleigh rides , and we had nice skiing. Down here at Potlatch one time, I know the kids had been coasting up and down the street, and our sled went right on around the horses and we got stuck right down here on one of these streets. Funny thing , we lost the halters to his horses and then his dad got at me for losing them!

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Did it ever occur to you not to get married?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: No . I decided to wait, my mother was married when she was 24, and I was gonna wait til she did . But I was 22 when I got married.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Do you remember the reasons why you got married?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: No. It was just time to get married, I guess.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: How did you feel after a year of marriage? Was marriage what you thought it was going to be before, when you were single?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Oh, sure. He was running the place for his mother then. His father had died and we moved out there with her and his three sisters. Then when she died, his mother moved to Moscow, put the girls in school. Then she died and I had the two girls, I guess they was 15 and 16, something like that.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: So you took care of your husband's sisters , then?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Yeah, and his brothers. He had some brothers . They always come home on weekends or something like that, always had lots of fun , all of them. His mother would come out from Moscow and spend the summer with us the first year ; then she died.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Did you enjoy that or did you think it was a lot of work?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: No , I enjoyed it. She liked to come out on the farm and we enjoyed her very much.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Did you feel any different after 10 years of marriage, or five years of marriage?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: It's still working. He hangs the bow on the old wall.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: How do you feel now about marriage?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Now? No, I wouldn't get married again, no.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Looking back on your marriage?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: I don't know how it could be any better. We enjoyed life. We were always happy together.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Did you ever have any discussion about whether you wanted children or not, you and your husband, whether to have children?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Not them days, you just took what come.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Did you have any interesting childbirth experiences that you'd like to share with us?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Oh no, I guess not.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Did you get much support from your husband when you were having the children?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Oh, you bet.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Was he a good father?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Oh, you bet.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: When your children were still young, did you have hopes or plans of what you wanted them to be?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: I wanted one of them to be a carpenter and none of them can drive a nail!

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Were you interested in carpentry yourself?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: No. I don't know, I just wanted one.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Good job. This, you kind of answered : what do you do for recreation and leisure time? You have a lot of clubs and societies that you belong to, plus a beautiful quilt .

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: That's just a [unintelligible].

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Oh, it is? You must have really high standards . It looks real good to me. What was the most significant thing you think you did in your life to support your family? Not just monetary, just in other ways that you helped. EC : I don't know. I just worked in the fields, at home, in the garden, chickens, and things like that .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: You had to work in the fields?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Oh yes, I loved that .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Did you enjoy that more than you enjoyed housework?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Yes, I always liked to be outside.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Do you have any idea how much trouble your family would have had to take if you hadn't been there, like the canning and the sewing, things like that, if they would have had to do? To hire another three people if you weren't there?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: I don't know, we never even thought of it . We just had our own work to do and if I had a headache or was sick or if we were very sick, I had to do it anyway, get their breakfast and stuff. I never trained my boys to wash dishes .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: You did the field work and then you'd come back and do housework too?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Yeah. Of course, he always took the kids out with him, when they were little bitsy things . He 'd take them out and put them to sleep on the machines he was working on, then he'd bring them in and put them to bed.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Do you think that if you had your life to live over again, to start again, would you do anything different, or would you do it the same?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: I suppose I would do it the same.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Who generally made the decisions in your family?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: He did. He always went ahead; he .was outside, I was inside. The house was mine, the barn was his .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Did he ever consult you when he had an important decision to make, talk it over a little bit?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: We always talked it over; but, whatever he said, I thought was all right. That's the way he did it . We always got along, that's one thing.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: How do you feel about living in a small rural area when you lived out there? Did you ever have a desire to live in a city? You wouldn't have liked to live in something like Spokane or Seattle?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: No, we lived there on the farm. He got the bad leg and we couldn't stay; then we moved to Lewiston. He got the bad leg when he bought this place and he died within the month. And he said that when he left there he wouldn't go back to the farm to get out and work because he had heart trouble.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Do you feel that your life is any different than women in the city?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: I think so. I don't think they would have done all that work. Of course, I had those extra youngsters I had to raise, other youngsters besides my own.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: The others besides your husband's brothers and sisters and your own children?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: I had his two sisters and my one boy. Then, my sister died and left two girls and I raised them. Then it was between my two boys, so I had them four . Then his sister died and left two more boys and I had them.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: That's a lot of children you raised.

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: He had an aunt, too, that I took care of before she died . I don't have much youngsters these days .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Do you like taking care of children?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Well, it just seemed to be my duty. There was nobody else to do it. Then my mother, she lived with me when she got real bad, she died of cancer.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Do you feel that your life was any different than your mother's life?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: I don't suppose so . She was like me, she was a farmer's wife and she took care of her family.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: How about your childrens' wives, do you feel they lead a different life than them?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: I have a wonderful daughter-in-law. This is one of my granddaughters , they live on my ranch there .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Oh yeah, I thought she probably was . In Princeton?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Yes .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Well, I think [unintelligible].

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: The neighbors had two teenage girls . We always took them to Whitmore. They used to drive our buggy and our [unintelligible]. We always had to drive four miles to get our telephone. The girls had to go out, my dad was working, so whenever there was a storm, we 'd pull up wherever there was a house and they'd give us shelter. They'd run into the house and they was already in the cellar, so they'd come out and help out the horses away. Them girls , one of them weighed about 300 and the other 250. They was down in that Edna Cochrane 18 old cellar and it rained. It rained in the old cellar and there was holes that the mice were in and it drowned the mice there, and one of the big girls was afraid of mice . They used to have those pickle barrels, you know those barrels, real big at the bottom, and she got up on one of them and was terrified and just screaming. When the storm was over, we looked out to see it was morning . We made a run for the house and the house had blown the roof off and the kitchen was just flooded with water, you know, from the windstorms . We had one of them in the farm house too . I was out in the yard and my mother said get those chickens, and they were just thrown it was a cyclone. We grabbed what we could and finally she said, "Well , get in the cellar." So we all run in the cellar, but my mother and my oldest brother, they sit down under some gooseberry bushes, and it blew the windmill and a 20 pound weight down where they had just sat up and moved . They thought they could make it to the house and when they had looked again, that weight had fell right where they'd been sitting; but they had moved, see. It blew our roof off and threw sticks through the window and glass blew into the house .

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: It must have been pretty exciting, a cyclone.

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Yeah. You always move to the cellar when there is a windstorm.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Haven't had real bad weather like that in Idaho , different types of weather.

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Get winds, but not a cyclone.

speaker: Jeanne Wood
words: Weather gets cold back there?

speaker: Edna Cochrane
words: Yes, it would get colder, but then it didn't freeze. It was dry cold, it wasn't wet cold.
